title: MYP Design eAssessment: Format, Criteria and Grades
summary: MYP Design eAssessment explained for Year 5 families: explore the ePortfolio format, four assessment criteria, moderation and how grades from 1 to 7 work.
body_markdown:
The **MYP Design eAssessment is an ePortfolio assessment, rather than a timed on-screen examination** . Students document how they investigate a need, develop ideas, create a solution and evaluate its success. Teachers assess that evidence against four criteria, and the IB externally moderates marking before awarding a subject grade from 1 to 7.


That distinction matters when a Year 5 student first hears the word “eAssessment”. It can suggest a countdown clock and unfamiliar questions. In Design, the challenge is different: making your thinking visible throughout a project.


Imagine a student developing a phone stand for someone who follows recipes while cooking. The finished stand matters. So do the research, rejected ideas, construction decisions and tests that explain whether it actually helps its user.


### MYP Design eAssessment at a glance


The IB’s[guidance on preparing ePortfolios](https://www.ibo.org/programmes/middle-years-programme/assessment-and-exams/e-portfolios/preparing-for-an-exam/) identifies Design among the subjects using partially completed unit planners. These provide the framework for the assessment undertaken through school.


Question What students and parents should know


Is there a Design on-screen exam? Design eAssessment uses an ePortfolio.


What is assessed? Evidence across the four Design criteria, A-D.


Who marks it? Teachers assess the work, with external IB moderation.


What is the scoring scale? Each criterion receives an achievement level from 0-8, giving a total out of 32.


What is the final result? An official subject grade from 1 to 7.


First, confirm that your school offers Design eAssessment and has registered you. Then ask for the assessment task, current submission requirements, deadlines and Year 5 criterion descriptors. RevisionDojo’s[MYP Design resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp/myp-design) provide a useful subject starting point alongside those school instructions.


### What does the ePortfolio involve?


An ePortfolio is a digital collection of evidence showing your response to an assessment task. It follows the design cycle, connecting an identified problem to a developed and tested solution.


The IB supplies a partially completed unit planner for each assessment session. Teachers use that framework to develop the assessment in their school. Consequently, a project found online may illustrate useful practice without matching your current task.


For our hypothetical student, the process could begin with observing a cook’s workspace. Does the phone slip? Is the screen difficult to read? Does the stand need to fold away? Those questions shape research and later become reasons for design decisions.


Save evidence as you work: research findings, annotated sketches, plans, photographs, test results and explanations of changes. Reconstructing everything at the end makes it harder to show how decisions developed. For a wider explanation of the process, see RevisionDojo’s[guide to the MYP ePortfolio](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-is-the-myp-eportfolio) .


A parent looks at a tiny phone stand beside a towering stack of design records while a student explains the documentation.


### The four MYP Design assessment criteria


Each criterion carries equal weight. A polished product alone cannot demonstrate everything the assessment asks students to show.


### Criterion A: Inquiring and analysing


Explain the need for a solution, plan relevant research, analyse existing products and develop a design brief from your findings.


For the phone stand, “people use phones” offers little direction. Observing a particular user and investigating stability, viewing angles and cleaning provides evidence that can guide a solution. RevisionDojo’s[notes on writing a design brief](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp/myp-design/myp-design-writing-a-design-brief/notes) help connect research to a clear statement of the problem.


### Criterion B: Developing ideas


Develop a design specification, communicate feasible ideas, justify your chosen design and prepare accurate planning drawings or diagrams.


A useful specification gives you something to test later. “Looks good” is difficult to evaluate consistently. A requirement based on the user’s available counter space or the dimensions of their phone gives your decisions a clearer purpose. Alternative ideas should reveal meaningful choices about function, materials or construction.


### Criterion C: Creating the solution


Produce a logical construction plan, demonstrate technical skills, follow the plan to create a functioning solution and justify changes made during production.


Record significant decisions while they are fresh. If the stand tips and you widen its base, explain what prompted the change. Photographs become stronger evidence when annotations identify the skill, difficulty or adjustment they demonstrate.


### Criterion D: Evaluating


Design relevant tests, evaluate the solution against your specification, explain improvements and consider its impact on the client or target audience.


Ask the intended user to complete a realistic task. Record what happens and connect the results to your success criteria. “The user liked it” provides less evidence than an observed test showing whether the screen stays readable and the stand remains stable.


### How are grades from 1 to 7 reached?


Teachers judge evidence against the Year 5 achievement descriptors for each criterion. Levels are organised into bands of 1-2, 3-4, 5-6 and 7-8, with 0 used when the work does not meet a described standard.


The four criterion levels produce a total out of 32. For example, A: 6, B: 5, C: 6 and D: 5 give a total of 22. That number is a criterion total, not yet an official subject grade.


External moderation checks the application of assessment standards and can lead to adjustments. The moderated result is converted into a grade from 1 to 7 using the applicable subject and session boundaries. Ask your coordinator for those boundaries rather than assuming a general school conversion chart guarantees your final result.


The IB’s[grading and awards guidance](https://www.ibo.org/programmes/middle-years-programme/assessment-and-exams/grading-and-awards/) explains the official reporting scale. RevisionDojo’s[MYP eAssessment grading guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-does-myp-eassessment-work) provides further context.


### Preparing well, with support that fits Design


At each checkpoint, identify the criterion you are addressing and the evidence still missing. Keep sources organised, explain decisions in your own words and leave time for testing before submission. Parents can help by asking, “What evidence supports that choice?” while keeping authorship with the student.


RevisionDojo brings Study Notes, Flashcards, a Questionbank and AI Chat into a broader IB study toolkit. Use relevant Design resources to clarify concepts and practise explaining decisions. Where available and permitted, Grading tools, the Coursework Library and Tutors can support feedback and understanding; your teacher’s instructions govern assessed work. Predicted Papers and Mock Exams serve other examination preparation needs, rather than replacing a Design portfolio.


As you organise Year 5 across subjects, RevisionDojo’s[MYP subject hub](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp) helps keep the different assessment demands in view. For Design, return to one practical question: can a reader follow the evidence from the user’s need to your evaluation? A clear answer gives your work its strongest foundation.
